title: Customer Expansion Signals: How to Act Without Pitching
summary: Customer expansion signals say when to write, not what to say. Why a note about usage limits can raise churn, and the outreach rules Outlit follows.
body_markdown:
## TL;dr


The customer about to run out of credits looks like your easiest upsell. Pitch them a bigger plan and you may lose them instead: it makes them look hard at what they're paying, and once they're choosing a plan, leaving is one of the options. Customer expansion signals like a usage limit, a run of pricing-page visits or a hiring push on the team that uses you are best used to decide when to write. What the note says should come from what the customer told you they're trying to do. We offer a choice, never just a bigger plan, and we don't ask the same customer again for two months.


Signal What it tells you What to do


Credits running out, plan pages opened, every seat in use, etc. When to write Offer a choice. Never mention the bill or the visits


Something they said they want: another team, more markets, a goal What to say Open on it, in their words


Hiring for the team that uses you, a new office, an acquisition, etc. Another team may need you Let it time the note. Ask about the new team


Funding, a new leader, a promoted champion, etc. Little on its own Look at the account. No note about the news


Seats or credits sitting unused They aren't getting what they pay for Help them use it. No growth note


## Which customer expansion signals are worth acting on?


Signals answer two different questions. Limits, full seats, page visits and company news, such as job posts for the team that uses you, answer when. The customer answers what: a goal named on a call, another team mentioned in a ticket, more markets they want to cover. When Outlit has their words, the note is built on them. Without them, the note can only say what their own account shows, such as credits running out before the reset, and never what Outlit watched.


The best customer to contact isn't the one most likely to buy. It's the one a note would actually move. A customer already growing on their own doesn't need the note, so Outlit leaves them alone. In retention,[Eva Ascarza found](https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2759170) that targeting the customers an offer actually moves beats targeting the ones most at risk, and the two are often different customers.


## Why can outreach about a usage limit backfire?


Because it asks the customer to make a decision they weren't going to make. In[Ascarza, Iyengar and Schleicher's field experiment](https://business.columbia.edu/sites/default/files-efs/pubfiles/12782/Perils_Ascarza.pdf) , a wireless carrier phoned customers who kept going over their allowance and offered a bigger plan that would have cut their bill. Over the next three months, 10% of them left, against 6% of customers who weren't called. Even an offer that saved them money made them look at what they used and paid, and broke the habit of simply staying.[Einav, Klopack and Mahoney](https://web.stanford.edu/~leinav/pubs/AER2025.pdf) saw the same in consumer subscriptions: people cancel about four times as often in the month a replaced card makes them decide again whether to keep paying.


A growth note that leads with the bill or a bigger plan does the same thing. It turns "keep going" into "decide again".


How often you ask matters too.[Güneş and colleagues](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/1094670509352677) modelled cross-selling at a retail bank on the premise that each failed attempt makes the next one less likely to land, and found the best time to ask again depends on how many attempts have already failed.


## What rules does Outlit follow when it writes a growth note?


Outlit drafts each note for the account owner, who sends it. These rules are part of the drafting itself:


1. **Start from what holds now, in their words where you have them.** A credit note opens on the credits running short. What they said, on a call, in an email or in a ticket in the last month, explains what the change is for, in their own words. Older words can still inform how Outlit reads the account, but a note that retells last spring's call as "you mentioned" tells them nobody was listening.
2. **Talk about their work, not their bill.** A note can say their credits are nearly used or that their plan rolls over next month. It never names what they pay, a price, a discount or a contract term, which is what sent the carrier's customers looking at their bill. A pricing question goes to a person.
3. **Never show what you watched.** Pricing-page visits, logins and day-to-day usage only decide when the note goes. A draft that reads as if Outlit watches them is rewritten, and dropped if it still does.
4. **Offer a choice, not an upgrade.** When credits will run out before they reset, the note gives two options when there are two, the best fit first: use a little less until the reset, add a top-up if you sell them, or move to a bigger plan. A bigger plan never appears on its own. A cheaper way to pay for the same thing, such as annual billing or a discount, doesn't grow the account, so it's never what a growth note asks for.
5. **Help them use what they have first.** If their credits are mostly unused, or something they pay for was never set up, there's no growth note. Selling more on top of unused capacity sets up a smaller renewal.
6. **One note, to the person who said it, from the owner.** It goes to the customer who raised what they want, or the champion, and never over their head. It comes from the owner's own mailbox or Slack, on whichever channel the customer already uses with you. For an account the owner runs, the note offers a call. For a self-serve account, it offers to set the change up. A note with credit options ends on the choice instead.
7. **Step back when someone else is already talking to them.** There's no note while a colleague's email or meeting is waiting on the customer, while a plan or price change is being worked out, or after anyone on your side followed up on the same topic.
8. **Ask once, then leave room.** A customer gets at most one growth note every 60 days.


## When should an expansion conversation wait?


Outlit holds back a growth note when:


- a renewal is being worked, so growth belongs in the[renewal conversation](https://www.outlit.ai/blog/how-to-run-your-renewal-process-with-outlit)
- a[rescue effort](https://www.outlit.ai/blog/helping-at-risk-customers) is under way or started recently
- something is unresolved on their side: an open complaint, doubts about value, a budget remark, a competitor under evaluation
- their champion changed in the last 60 days, so you help the new person first
- there's news of layoffs, or several of their people left at once
- they haven't reached first value, which makes it[onboarding work](https://www.outlit.ai/blog/stalled-onboarding)


## How can a SaaS company grow long-tail revenue without waiting for customers to request an upgrade?


On a long tail, nobody hears the goal a customer mentions in a support ticket, nobody notices the credits running out the same week, and nobody sees the job posts for the team that uses you. Outlit reads every account for all of it, then writes the note an owner would write with time to look: the customer's words, a real choice, nothing about their bill. Without that, expansion depends on customers asking, one cost of[covering a large book with a small team](https://www.outlit.ai/blog/when-to-move-to-scaled-customer-success) .


### Worked example


An illustrative account, not a customer record. Today is Monday Nov 16 .


- **What they said:** on Nov 4 , in a Pylon


ticket about permissions, their ops lead mentioned that the sales team starts using the product in December.
- **What changed:** at the current pace, Stripe


shows their monthly credits running out on Nov 24 , six days before they reset. Their admin has opened the plans page on three days since Thursday, and they've posted two sales rep roles.
- **Why nothing stops it:** nobody on your side has followed up on the sales team, no renewal is being worked, and their last growth note was in June.
- **Decision:** a draft for the owner to send to the ops lead. It opens on the credits running out a few days before the reset, ties that to the sales team joining in December, and offers two options: a top-up to cover the six days, or the next plan up, which also covers December. It ends by asking which they'd prefer. It carries no price and says nothing about the plans page or the job posts.
- **Next check:** the ops lead's reply, a top-up or plan change in Stripe


, or the reset on Nov 30 .


## How do you know it's working?


For each kind of signal, over at least one billing cycle, count notes sent, replies, and top-ups, plan changes and added seats in billing. Then compare churn among customers who got a note with similar customers who didn't. A growth note that raises churn is losing money even when some customers upgrade. Before trusting a rule, run it by hand on last quarter: take the accounts that bought more and a similar set that didn't, and count how many buyers the rules would have caught and how many notes an owner would have thrown away.


## Where does Outlit fit?


Outlit runs these rules on every account, every day. It[matches](https://www.outlit.ai/blog/what-is-customer-context-infrastructure) billing, product usage, support, CRM, email, Slack and calls to the right customer, and watches each customer's public news: funding, hiring, launches and leadership changes. What passes reaches the owner through an inbox that decides each day what deserves attention, with the evidence and a draft attached. Growth notes reach the owner as drafts to send. See how Outlit[helps customers buy more](https://www.outlit.ai/use-cases/expansion) .
